transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

Now that I’m supposed to be slowing down, I feel like I’m always on the go and can’t just sit still and relax, even for a short visit or a quiet meal. Since I started transitioning into partial retirement, this constant need to be in motion has become really noticeable and quite uncomfortable.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'can't just sit still' - are you experiencing restlessness, fidgeting, or an inability to remain seated for periods of time?

Yes, I'm constantly fidgeting—bouncing my feet, drumming my fingers, and shifting in my seat without even realizing it. Staying seated for a whole meal or meeting feels almost unbearable, so I'll constantly pop up to refill water or clear plates just to keep moving. It really feels like this pent-up energy inside me that won't let me just sit and relax.
Do you feel anxious or stressed when you're unable to move around or engage in physical activity, or is it more about the physical discomfort of being still?

It is definitely more about the physical discomfort and a constant urge to stay in motion rather than emotional anxiety or worry. When I try to sit still, I get this odd agitation and a build-up of pent-up energy that makes staying seated feel almost unbearable. While I initially worried it might be anxiety, it really feels like a physical sensation pushing me to get up.
Have you noticed any involuntary movements, such as twitching or jerking, in addition to the restlessness and fidgeting you've described?

No, I haven't noticed any involuntary twitching or jerking at all. It's more of a semi-conscious fidgeting, like tapping my fingers or bouncing my foot, driven by that constant urge to stay in motion rather than any kind of muscle spasm.

You mentioned this started becoming noticeable when you began transitioning into partial retirement; has the severity of these symptoms remained constant since then, or have you noticed any fluctuations?

They have been consistently noticeable over the past eight months since I started partial retirement. The severity definitely fluctuates depending on how much structure I have; on days when I have a tight teaching schedule I feel much more anchored, but on unstructured days at home, the restlessness and constant motion become much more pronounced.

Can you describe how your restlessness and urge to move are affected by engaging in mentally stimulating activities versus physical exercise, and do either of these types of activities provide you with any relief from your symptoms?

I haven't really thought about comparing mental stimulation versus physical exercise, and I'm not sure if either actually provides true relief. Instead, I just naturally gravitate toward staying busy with hands-on tasks like gardening, organizing, or planning events to cope with my pent-up energy. Because of that, I don't really have a clear answer on how structured exercise or pure mental tasks affect the restlessness differently.

When you engage in physical activities like gardening or organizing, does the restlessness and urge to move decrease for a while after you've been active, or does it not seem to have a lasting impact on your symptoms?

While I'm actively gardening or reorganizing, those tasks keep me occupied in the moment. But the second I sit down to rest, that pent-up energy and the urge to move return immediately. Being active doesn't seem to provide any lasting relief once I stop.

You've mentioned that these symptoms became more noticeable during your transition to partial retirement; did you experience any similar feelings of restlessness or need to be constantly in motion earlier in your life, or is this a relatively new development?

This is actually a lifelong pattern rather than a brand-new issue, though it has become much more noticeable now without my rigid school schedule. Even back in primary school, teachers always told my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, was constantly chatting, and kept popping up to sharpen my pencil or wander around while others worked quietly. It has definitely been there since childhood, but having a highly structured teaching career helped me keep a lid on it for a long time.

You mentioned this restlessness has been a lifelong pattern, but it's become more noticeable since your transition to partial retirement. Did you exhibit any other symptoms in childhood, such as inattention or impulsivity, that might have been related to this restlessness?

Yes, it was definitely more on the impulsive and hyperactive side rather than having trouble paying attention. Even back in primary school, my teachers were constantly complaining to my parents about me chatting with classmates, interrupting, and always finding excuses to get out of my seat to wander the room.

You've mentioned impulsivity and hyperactivity, but can you tell me more about your ability to focus and pay attention, both as a child and now, and whether you've ever had difficulty with tasks that require sustained mental effort?

I haven't really noticed any significant issues with focusing or paying attention, either now or when I was a child. My main struggle has always been the physical restlessness and keeping still, rather than an inability to concentrate on the tasks themselves.

Given that you've had symptoms of restlessness and hyperactivity since childhood, did you ever receive any diagnosis or treatment for these symptoms when you were younger, or were they simply managed through your structured school and work environments?

No, I was never diagnosed or treated when I was younger; back then, my constant moving and chatting were just seen as behavioral quirks rather than a medical issue. I managed to cope throughout my life because my career as a teacher kept me anchored in a highly structured environment with tight bell schedules and constant agendas. It is only now, with the loss of that daily structure in retirement, that these symptoms have become truly difficult to manage.

Can you confirm that your symptoms of restlessness, fidgeting, and hyperactivity have been consistently present since childhood, rather than starting in adulthood, and have persisted into adulthood despite some periods of better management due to structured environments?

Yes, I can absolutely confirm that these behaviors definitely go back to my childhood. Even in primary school, my teachers constantly told my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat, was always chatting, and kept getting up to sharpen pencils or wander around. Having a highly structured teaching career helped me manage and mask it for decades, but easing into retirement has made these lifelong tendencies highly visible again.

Have you experienced any significant reduction in your restlessness or hyperactivity symptoms at any point in your life, even temporarily, or have they consistently been present despite some periods of better management?

No, they have been consistently present throughout my entire life without any real breaks. However, they were much better managed and less noticeable when I had the strict structure of my teaching job with its tight bell schedules and constant meetings. Since transitioning toward retirement eight months ago and losing that daily routine, the restlessness has become far more pronounced and difficult to handle.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood and have persisted into adulthood, but can you clarify if you've ever experienced any periods, even brief, where you felt completely free of these symptoms, or have they always been present to some degree?

No, I have never been completely free of them; this tendency to be in motion has always been present to some degree since my childhood. During my years as a full-time teacher, the highly structured environment of school bell schedules and constant agendas kept me anchored, which made the symptoms less disruptive. They never truly went away, but they became much more noticeable and harder to manage once that professional structure disappeared eight months ago.

You mentioned you didn't have significant issues with focusing or paying attention, but can you think of any situations, either in the past or currently, where you had difficulty following through on instructions, finishing tasks, or making careless mistakes due to lack of attention to details?

I can't really recall ever having those kinds of issues with attention, following instructions, or making careless mistakes. My challenges have always been much more about my physical restlessness and struggling to stay still, rather than any difficulty with focusing or finishing my tasks.

Can you think of any instances where you might have had difficulty with organization, time management, or forgetfulness, which could be related to aspects of inattention, even if you didn't have issues with focusing or paying attention?

I don't really recall having any significant issues with organization, time management, or forgetfulness. Those areas have never really been a major struggle for me, and I've always been able to keep on top of my schedule and responsibilities quite well.

Can you describe how your symptoms of restlessness and hyperactivity have impacted your daily life and relationships, and have you noticed any differences in how these symptoms manifest in different social or professional settings?

My inability to sit still has turned relaxing social events like my book club and family dinners into stressful experiences, and my husband gets irritated that I can't just stay present without constantly jumping up to do things. While the tight schedules and structured agendas at school previously kept me anchored and masked my restlessness, the unstructured days of partial retirement have made this constant need to be in motion much more obvious and difficult to manage.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood and have persisted into adulthood; can you confirm if there was ever a period, even brief, where these symptoms significantly diminished or remitted, or have they been consistently present throughout your life?

No, they have never really gone away; they have been consistently present since my childhood. They were simply kept in check and masked for decades by the highly structured environment of my teaching career. Since cutting back on work eight months ago and losing that daily structure, this lifelong restlessness has become much more pronounced and harder to manage.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood, but can you confirm if you've experienced any periods of significant reduction in symptoms during adulthood, particularly before your transition to partial retirement, that might help differentiate between possible diagnoses?

I'm not quite sure, as I haven't really thought about my symptoms in terms of "reductions." I don't recall any specific periods where these feelings completely went away, but rather my highly structured teaching routine kept me too busy to focus on them as a major issue until now.

Have you experienced any symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following instructions or making careless mistakes, in addition to your restlessness and hyperactivity, or have these symptoms been relatively absent throughout your life?

Those kinds of inattention issues have been relatively absent throughout my entire life. I have never really struggled with making careless mistakes or following instructions. My difficulties have always been completely focused on my physical restlessness, staying still, and feeling constantly on the go.

Can you clarify if your restlessness is primarily driven by a desire to be active and engaged, or if it's also associated with impulsive behaviors, such as interrupting others or acting without thinking?

It is actually a combination of both; when I try to sit still, I get a pent-up energy that physically drives me to find tasks like gardening or reorganizing. At the same time, I definitely struggle with impulsivity, often catching myself interrupting others or finishing my husband's sentences before realizing I've cut them off.

Can you describe any recent instances where your impulsivity led to problems in your daily life or relationships, such as interrupting others or acting on impulse without considering the consequences?

Yes, I frequently jump into people's sentences during meetings and constantly finish my husband's thoughts at home, blurting out what I'm thinking before they can finish. I only realize afterward that I've cut them off or shifted the focus to myself, which has started to irritate my husband and make social interactions feel quite strained.

Have you ever experienced any significant problems at work or in personal relationships due to your impulsivity, such as interrupting others or blurting out answers, and if so, can you describe a recent instance?

Yes, I definitely struggle with that. During staff meetings at school, I often catch myself jumping into my colleagues' sentences, and at home, I constantly find myself finishing my husband's thoughts before he can get them out. I only realize afterward that I've cut them off or shifted the focus to my own ideas, which has started to cause some real irritation and strain in my relationships.
Can you think of any situations where your impulsivity led to more serious consequences, such as conflicts or accidents, rather than just social awkwardness or irritation?

No, I really can't think of any serious consequences like accidents or major conflicts. The issues have mostly been limited to the daily frustrations, social awkwardness, and the irritation from my husband and friends that I've already described.
Can you think of any situations where you acted impulsively without fully considering the consequences, and if so, can you describe what happened?

My impulsiveness is really limited to conversations and meetings rather than anything dangerous. I constantly catch myself jumping into other people's sentences or finishing my husband's thoughts, blurting out my ideas before they can finish. It's only afterward that I realize I've interrupted them or completely derailed the conversation without meaning to.

Have you ever experienced any symptoms of inattention or disorganization, such as difficulty keeping track of tasks or forgetting important items, in addition to your restlessness, hyperactivity, and impulsivity?

No, I haven't really struggled with inattention, disorganization, or forgetting things at all. My difficulties have always been focused on my physical restlessness, constant activity, and trouble sitting still.

Can you describe how your symptoms of restlessness, hyperactivity, and impulsivity have impacted your daily life and relationships differently across various settings, such as at home, in social situations, or in more structured environments like your previous teaching job?

When I was teaching, the strict school bells and agendas kept me anchored, though I still fidgeted and interrupted colleagues during staff meetings. Now, without that structure, my constant need to jump up has started to irritate my husband at home, and social gatherings like book club or family dinners have become stressful instead of relaxing. It is as if the lack of a schedule has made my lifelong restlessness much harder to hide and manage.
Can you describe a situation where you exhibited hyperactive behavior without being impulsive, such as engaging in excessive running or climbing without interrupting others or acting out of turn?

Well, at my age, I'm certainly not running or climbing on things, but I experience that physical hyperactivity by constantly staying in motion, like spending hours weeding the garden or reorganizing closets to burn off pent-up energy. During family dinners or book clubs, I'll constantly get up to refill water or clear plates simply because sitting still feels unbearable, which is a purely physical need to move rather than being impulsive or trying to disrupt anyone.

Can you think of any times when you felt restless or fidgety without also feeling the urge to interrupt others or act impulsively, which might help clarify whether your symptoms are primarily hyperactive or a combination of hyperactivity and impulsivity?

Yes, definitely. When I am alone at home trying to read or watch a movie, I feel an intense, pent-up physical energy that forces me to fidget or get up to weed the garden or reorganize closets, even though there is no one around to talk to or interrupt. It is really only in social settings where both that physical restlessness and the urge to blurt things out tend to happen together.

Can you confirm whether your symptoms of restlessness and hyperactivity have always been accompanied by impulsivity, or if there have been periods where you experienced restlessness without impulsivity?

I'm not quite sure and haven't really thought about whether they have always gone hand-in-hand. However, both the constant need to move and my tendency to blurt things out or interrupt have been very noticeable parts of my life, especially recently since I've cut back on my teaching structure.
